title: Study Guide for Unit 1
text:
2. One-Sample (\(z\)) Test for a Mean
Use when the population standard deviation (\(\sigma\)) is known.

Test Statistic
\[
z=\frac{\bar{x}-\mu_0}{\sigma/\sqrt{n}}
\]
where:

\(\bar{x}\) = sample mean
\(\mu_0\) = hypothesized population mean
\(\sigma\) = population standard deviation
\(n\) = sample size

z <- (xbar - mu0) / (sigma / sqrt(n))


P-Value
# Left-tailed
pnorm(z)

# Right-tailed
1 - pnorm(z)

# Two-tailed
2 * (1 - pnorm(abs(z)))


Critical Values
# Left-tailed
qnorm(alpha)

# Right-tailed
qnorm(1 - alpha)

# Two-tailed
qnorm(1 - alpha / 2)

title: Study Guide for Unit 1
text:
3. One-Sample (t) Test for a Mean
Use when the population standard deviation is unknown and \(s\) is used instead.

Test Statistic
\[
t=\frac{\bar{x}-\mu_0}{s/\sqrt{n}}
\]


Degrees of Freedom
\[
df=n-1
\]
df <- n - 1

t_stat <- (xbar - mu0) / (s / sqrt(n))


P-Value
# Left-tailed
pt(t_stat, df)

# Right-tailed
1 - pt(t_stat, df)
pt(t_stat, df, lower.tail = FALSE)

# Two-tailed
2 * pt(-abs(t_stat), df)


Critical Values
# Left-tailed
qt(alpha, df)

# Right-tailed
qt(1 - alpha, df)
qt(alpha, df, lower.tail = FALSE)

# Two-tailed
qt(1 - alpha / 2, df)

title: Study Guide for Unit 1
section: 4. Confidence Interval for a Population Mean
text:
4. Confidence Interval for a Population Mean

When \(\sigma\) Is Known
\[
\bar{x}\pm z_{\alpha/2}\frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}
\]
z_critical <- qnorm(1 - alpha / 2)

margin_error <- z_critical * sigma / sqrt(n)

lower <- xbar - margin_error
upper <- xbar + margin_error


When \(\sigma\) Is Unknown
\[
\bar{x}\pm t_{\alpha/2,df}\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}
\]
with:
\[
df=n-1
\]
df <- n - 1

t_critical <- qt(1 - alpha / 2, df)

margin_error <- t_critical * s / sqrt(n)

lower <- xbar - margin_error
upper <- xbar + margin_error

c(lower = lower, upper = upper)


CI for a Two-Tailed Test
For:
\[
H_0:\mu=\mu_0
\]

If \(\mu_0\) is inside the confidence interval, fail to reject \(H_0\).
If \(\mu_0\) is outside the confidence interval, reject \(H_0\).

title: Study Guide for Unit 1
text:
5. One-Proportion \(z\) Test
Use when testing a population proportion.

Sample Proportion
\[
\hat{p}=\frac{x}{n}
\]
p_hat <- x / n
where \(x\) is the number with the characteristic of interest.


Check the Conditions
Both should be at least 5:
\[
np_0\ge5
\]
\[
n(1-p_0)\ge5
\]
n * p0
n * (1 - p0)


Test Statistic
\[
z=
\frac{\hat{p}-p_0}
{\sqrt{\frac{p_0(1-p_0)}{n}}}
\]
z <- (p_hat - p0) /
     sqrt(p0 * (1 - p0) / n)
Then use the same pnorm() commands as any other \(z\) test:
# Left-tailed
pnorm(z)

# Right-tailed
1 - pnorm(z)
pnorm(z, lower.tail = FALSE)

# Two-tailed
2 * (1 - pnorm(abs(z)))

title: Study Guide for Unit 1
section: 6. Chi-Square Test for a Population Variance
text:
6. Chi-Square Test for a Population Variance
Use when testing a population variance or standard deviation.
If standard deviations are given, convert them to variance:
\[
s^2=(s)^2
\]
\[
\sigma_0^2=(\sigma_0)^2
\]
s^2
sigma0^2

Test Statistic
\[
\chi^2=
\frac{(n-1)s^2}{\sigma_0^2}
\]


Degrees of Freedom
\[
df=n-1
\]
df <- n - 1

chi_square <- (n - 1) * s^2 / sigma0^2


Critical Values
# Left-tailed
qchisq(alpha, df)

# Right-tailed
qchisq(1 - alpha, df)
qchisq(alpha, df, lower.tail = FALSE)

# Two-tailed
lower <- qchisq(alpha / 2, df)
upper <- qchisq(1 - alpha / 2, df)


P-Values
# Left-tailed
pchisq(chi_square, df)

# Right-tailed
1 - pchisq(chi_square, df)
pchisq(chi_square, df, lower.tail = FALSE)

title: exam3
text:
Uniform Distribution

Identification
Problem gives:

the variable is uniformly distributed
values lie between \(a\) and \(b\)
every value in the interval is equally likely



Key formulas
Mean:
\[
\mu = \frac{a+b}{2}
\]
Standard deviation
\[
\sigma = \sqrt{\frac{(b-a)^2}{12}}
\]
Probability to the right of a cutoff:
\[
P(X > x) = \frac{b-x}{b-a}
\]
Probability to the left of a cutoff:
\[
P(X < x) = \frac{x-a}{b-a}
\]


Example script

# mean and standard deviation
mu <- (a + b) / 2
sigma <- sqrt((b - a)^2 / 12)

# probability greater than x
(b - x) / (b - a)

# probability less than x
(x - a) / (b - a)

title: exam3
section: Normal distribution with a single raw score
text:
Normal distribution with a single raw score

Identification
Problem gives:

a mean and standard deviation
says that the variable is normally distributed
asks about a randomly selected observation
uses \(X\) rather than \(\bar{x}\)



Key formulas
For a value between two numbers:
\[
P(a < X < b)
\]
Standardizing:
\[
P(a < X < b)
\]
For a value above a cutoff:
\[
P(X > x)
\]
For a value below a cutoff:
\[
P(X < x)
\]
For finding a cutoff from a percentile:
\[
P(X \le x) = p
\]
For solving for standard deviation:
\[
z = \frac{x - \mu}{\sigma}\qquad \Rightarrow \qquad\sigma = \frac{x - \mu}{z}
\]


Example script 

# between two values
pnorm(upper, mean = mu, sd = sigma) - 
  pnorm(lower, mean = mu, sd = sigma)

# greater than
1 - pnorm(x, mean = mu, sd = sigma)

# less than
pnorm(x, mean = mu, sd = sigma)

# cutoff from a percentile
qnorm(p, mean = mu, sd = sigma)

# solve for sigma
z <- qnorm(p_left)
sigma <- (x - mu) / z

title: exam3
text:
Graphs of Normal Distributions

Identification
Conceptual problems comparing:

centers of the curves
width/spread of the curves
whether means are the same or different
whether standard deviations are the same or different



Key ideas
\[
\text{Different centers} \Rightarrow \text{different means}\\
\text{Wider/flatter curve} \Rightarrow \text{larger standard deviation}\\
\text{Narrower/taller curve} \Rightarrow \text{smaller standard deviation}
\]

title: exam3
text:
Empirical Rule

Identification
Problem shows:

a normal curve
shaded regions
labels involving 𝜇, 𝜇 + 𝜎, 𝜇 + 2𝜎, 𝜇 + 3𝜎



Key ideas
\[
68\% \text{ is within } \mu \pm \sigma\\
95\% \text{ is within } \mu \pm 2\sigma\\
99.7\% \text{ is within } \mu \pm 3\sigma
\]


Supporting Script

curve(dnorm(x), from = -4, to = 4)
abline(v = c(0, 1, 2, 3), lty = 2)

title: exam3
text:
Sampling distribution of the mean \(\bar{X}\)

Identification
Problem gives:

“sample mean”
“a random sample of \(n\)”
“what is the probability that the sample mean…”
“sampling distribution”



Key formulas
Mean of the sampling distribution:
\[
\mu_{\bar{X}} = \mu
\]
Standard deviation of the sampling distribution, also called the standard error:
\[
\sigma_{\bar{X}} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}
\]
If variance is given first:
\[
\sigma = \sqrt{\text{variance}}\\
\sigma_{\bar{X}} = \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}
\]
Probability forms:
\[
P(\bar{X} < x)\\
P(\bar{X} > x)\\
P\bigl(|\bar{X} - \mu| < a\bigr)\\
P\bigl(|\bar{X} - \mu| > a\bigr)
\]
Expanded interval forms:
\[
P(\mu - a < \bar{X} < \mu + a)\\
P(\bar{X} < \mu - a) + P(\bar{X} > \mu + a)
\]


Example script

# if variance is given
sigma <- sqrt(variance)

# standard error
se <- sigma / sqrt(n)

# less than
pnorm(xbar, mean = mu, sd = se)

# greater than
1 - pnorm(xbar, mean = mu, sd = se)

# within a distance of mu
pnorm(mu + amount, mean = mu, sd = se) -
  pnorm(mu - amount, mean = mu, sd = se)

# greater than a distance from mu
1 - (pnorm(mu + amount, mean = mu, sd = se) -
       pnorm(mu - amount, mean = mu, sd = se))

title: Exam 1 Formula Guide
text:
Frequency Tables
Relative frequency is:
\[
\text{Relative Frequency} = \frac{f}{n}
\]
Percentage is:
\[
\text{Percentage} = \frac{f}{n}\times 100
\]
where \(f\) is the frequency and nn is the total number of observations.

install.packages("descr") #install the package *once* if you chose to use this option
library(descr) # load the package from your library
descr::freq(as.ordered(data$variable), plot = FALSE) # function freq()


x <- c("A", "A", "B", "B", "B", "C")

freq <- table(x)
n <- length(x)

freq                    # Frequency
freq / n                # Relative frequency
(freq / n) * 100        # Percentage
cumsum(freq)            # Cumulative frequency

title: Exam 1 Formula Guide
text:
Central Tendency

Mode

library(lsr)


lsr::modeOf(data$variable, na.rm = TRUE)


# Simple histogram
x <- c(13,13,-5,-5,13,11,-5)
hist(x, breaks = 10)           # breaks = bins = classes



Median

x <- c(13,13,-5,-5,13,11,-5)
median(x)


median(data$variable, na.rm = TRUE)



Mean
The arithmetic mean is:
\[
\bar{x} = \frac{\sum x_i}{n}
\]
where \(\bar{x}\) is the sample mean, \(x_i\) represents each observation, and \(n\) is the number of observations.

(56 + 31 + 56 + 8 + 32) / 5


x <- c(13,13,-5,-5,13,11,-5)
sum(x) / length(x)


x <- c(56, 31, 56, 8, 32)
mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)



Weighted Mean
The weighted mean is:
\[
\bar{x}_w = \frac{\sum w_i x_i}{\sum w_i}
\]
where \(x_i\) is each observation and \(w_i\) is its corresponding weight.

# Weighted Mean
x <- c(24, 41, 58, 75, 92) # observations
w <- c(2, 8, 15, 8, 11)    # weights

sum(x * w) / sum(w)


# Weighted Mean Function
x <- c(24, 41, 58, 75, 92) # observations
w <- c(2, 8, 15, 8, 11)    # weights

weighted.mean(x, w, na.rm = TRUE)

The weighted sample variance is:
\[
s^2 = \frac{\sum w_i(x_i-\bar{x}_w)^2}{n-1}
\]
where \(n = \sum w_i\).

# variance, calculate after calculating the mean
x <- c(24, 41, 58, 75, 92) # observations
w <- c(2, 8, 15, 8, 11)    # weights

n <- sum(w)

xbar <- sum(x * w) / n                   # weighted mean
s2   <- sum(w * (x - xbar)^2) / (n - 1)  # sample, weighted variance

xbar
s2



Trimmed Mean

x <- c(0.32, 0.33, 0.36, 0.36, 0.39, 0.41, 0.49, 0.57, 0.6, 0.62, 0.63, 0.65, 0.65, 0.68, 0.72, 0.73, 0.76, 0.77, 0.78, 0.79)
mean(x, trim = .2)

title: Exam 1 Formula Guide
text:
Dispersion

Range
The range is:
\[
\text{Range} = x_{\max} - x_{\min}
\]

x <- c(30, 20, 10, 50, 100)

max_mass <- max(x, na.rm = TRUE)
min_mass <- min(x, na.rm = TRUE)

max_mass - min_mass


range(data$variable, na.rm = TRUE)
range(x)
# Then max - min



Variance
For a population:
\[
\sigma^2 = \frac{\sum (x_i-\mu)^2}{N}
\]
where \(\mu\) is the population mean and \(N\) is the population size.

# Population Variance
x <- c(24, 41, 58, 75, 92)

xbar <- mean(x)

variance <- sum((x - xbar)^2) / (length(x)) # use n
variance

For a sample:
\[
s^2 = \frac{\sum (x_i-\bar{x})^2}{n-1}
\]
where \(\bar{x}\) is the sample mean and \(n\) is the sample size.

# Sample Variance
x <- c(24, 41, 58, 75, 92)

xbar <- mean(x)

variance <- sum((x - xbar)^2) / (length(x) - 1) # use n - 1
variance


# Sample Variance Function
var(x)



MAD

# Not tested.



Standard Deviation
Standard deviation is the square root of variance:
\[
s = \sqrt{s^2}
\]
For a population:
\[
\sigma = \sqrt{\frac{\sum (x_i-\mu)^2}{N}}
\]

# Population Standard Deviation
x <- c(600, 470, 170, 430, 300)

xbar <- mean(x)
variance <- sum((x - xbar)^2) / length(x)
SD <- sqrt(variance)
SD


# Sample Standard Deviation
x <- c(600, 470, 170, 430, 300)

xbar <- mean(x)
variance <- sum((x - xbar)^2) / (length(x) - 1)
SD <- sqrt(variance)
SD


# Sample Standard Deviation Function
x <- c(600, 470, 170, 430, 300)

sd(x)

title: Exam 1 Formula Guide
text:
Relative Positioning

z-scores
The z-score is:
\[
z = \frac{x-\mu}{\sigma}
\]
where \(x\) is the observed value, \(\mu\) is the mean, and \(\sigma\) is the standard deviation.

score <- 46.9
mu    <- 43.6
SD    <- 4.7

zscore <- (score - mu) / SD
zscore



Percentiles

x <- c(6.1, 9.1, 9.5, 6, 8.6, 6.2, 9.1, 6.1, 8, 5.7, 6.5)

# One at a time
quantile(x, .28)

# Several at once
quantile(duration, c(.32, .57, .98))



Quartiles

x <- c(10, 11, 13, 14, 14, 16, 17, 20, 25, 26, 26, 26, 27, 30, 33, 33, 33, 35, 38, 41, 41, 44, 44, 45, 45, 46)

x <- sort(x)
n <- length(x)

if (n %% 2 == 0) {
  lower <- x[1:(n/2)]
  upper <- x[(n/2 + 1):n]
} else {
  lower <- x[1:((n - 1) / 2)]
  upper <- x[((n + 3) / 2):n]
}

title: Exam 1 Formula Guide
text:
Two Variables

Covariance
The sample covariance is:
\[
s_{xy}
=
\frac{\sum (x_i-\bar{x})(y_i-\bar{y})}{n-1}
\]
A positive covariance indicates that the variables tend to move in the same direction, while a negative covariance indicates that they tend to move in opposite directions.

x <- c(0.5, 1, 1.5, 2, 3, 3.5, 4, 4.5, 5.5, 6)
y <- c(63,  66, 69, 72, 78, 81, 84, 87, 90, 96)

# x
xbar <- mean(x)
xn   <- length(x)
xSD  <- sqrt( (sum((x - xbar)^2)) / (length(x)-1) ) # sample is n - 1

# y
ybar <- mean(y)
ySD  <- sqrt( (sum((y - ybar)^2)) / (length(y)-1) ) # sample is n - 1
yn   <- length(y)

# covariance
covariance <- (sum((x - xbar)*(y - ybar)) / (length(x)-1) )

covariance


# using data
cov(x = data$x, y = data$y)

# using vectors
cov(x, y)



Correlation Coefficient
The correlation coefficient can be calculated from the covariance and standard deviations:
\[
r = \frac{s_{xy}}{s_xs_y}
\]
where \(s_{xy}\) is the sample covariance and \(s_x\) and \(s_y\) are the sample standard deviations.

# REQUIRED: Use the covariance section above AND run it !
# Then, calculate r
r <- covariance / (xSD * ySD)
r


# using data
cor(x = data$x, y = data$y)

# using vectors
cor(x, y)

Recognizing the problem







Clue in the problem

title: Exam 2 Review
text:
Probability rules
The sample space is the set of all possible outcomes. An event is a subset of those outcomes.

Basic Probability
When individual outcomes are equally likely:
\[
P(A) = \frac{\text{number of favorable outcomes}}{\text{total number of outcomes}}
\]

x / y


favorable <- 3
total     <- 6

favorable / total



Unions (A or B)
\[
P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B)
\]
Subtract the overlap because it is counted in both \(P(A)\) and \(P(B)\). For mutually exclusive events, the overlap is zero.

total  <- NA
n_A    <- NA
n_B    <- NA
n_both <- NA

(n_A + n_B - n_both) / total  



Conditional Probability (A given B)
\[
P(A\mid B)=\frac{P(A\cap B)}{P(B)},\qquad P(B)>0.
\]
The condition changes the reference group to the outcomes in \(B\).
The denominator is the count or probability for the event after the words given that. In general, \(P(A\mid B)\) and \(P(B\mid A)\) can differ.
Using counts from the same group, divide the number in both events by the number in the conditioning event.

n_both <- 6
n_B    <- 14

n_both / n_B



Intersections (A and B)

Independence
\[
P(A \cap B) = P (A\;and\;B) = P(A) \times P(B)
\]

p_A <- 1 / 2
p_B <- 1 / 6

p_A * p_B



Dependent (General Multiplication Rule)
\[
P(A \cap B) = P (A\;and\;B)= P(A) \times P(B \vert A)
\]

p_A  <- 5 / 8
p_BA <- 4 / 7

p_A * p_BA




Complement
\[
P(A^c)= P (not\;A) = 1 - P(A)
\]

p_A <- NA

1 - p_A

title: Exam 2 Review
text:
Discrete Random Variable
List each possible numerical value with its probability. Probabilities must be between 0 and 1 and sum to 1.

Expected Value
The expected value is the long-run average over many repetitions. It does not have to be a possible value of \(X\).
\[
E(X) = \sum_{i} x_i \, P(X = x_i)
\]

# Possible values and their matching probabilities
x    <- c(   0,    1,    2)
prob <- c(0.20, 0.50, 0.30)

mu <- sum(x * prob)
mu



Variance and Standard Deviation
\[
\mathrm{Var}(X) = \sum_{i} (x_i - \mu)^2 \, P(X = x_i)\\\sigma = \sqrt{\mathrm{Var}(X)}
\]

variance <- sum((x - mu)^2 * prob)
variance

standard_deviation <- sqrt(variance)
standard_deviation

A factorial multiplies the positive integers up to \(n\):
\[ n!=n(n-1)\cdots2(1),\qquad 0!=1. \]
When selecting \(r\) objects from \(n\) distinct objects without regard to order:
\[ \binom{n}{r}=\frac{n!}{r!(n-r)!}. \]

Binomial Distribution
Counts successes in \(n\) trials: a fixed number of trials, two outcomes per trial, independent trials, and a constant success probability \(p\). “Success” is the outcome being counted.

\]

title: Exam 2 Review
text:
Poisson Distribution
Counts events in a fixed interval of time, length, area, or volume.
\[
P(X = x) = \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^x}{x!}, \quad x = 0,1,2,\ldots
\]
where

\(e \approx 2.71828\)
In R, we can use exp(-lambda)
\(\lambda\) (lambda; Greek) = mean number of occurrences for the specified interval
\(x\) = number of events
\(x!\) (factorial) = means multiply all whole numbers from \(x\) down to 1
\(x! = x \times (x - 1) ... \times 1\)
In R, we will use factorial(a)

For a Poisson distribution:
\[ \mu = \sigma^2 = \lambda \]
The mean equals the variance which equals \(\lambda\). So, \(\lambda\) controls both the center and spread of the distribution.

title: Exam 2 Review
text:
Hypergeometric Distribution
Counts successes in a random sample drawn without replacement from a finite population with known successes and failures. Every sample of the given size is equally likely.
\[
P(X = x) = \frac{\binom{k}{x}\binom{N-k}{\,n-x\,}}{\binom{N}{n}}
\]
where

\(k\) = the total number of successes possible in the population
\(N\) = the size of the total population
\(n\) = the size of the sample drawn
\(x\) = the number of successes in the sample of size \(n\)

  choose(N, sample_size)

  x = NA, # number of successes in sample
  m = NA, # number of successes in population

  k = NA  # sample size

Expected Value
The expected value tells us the average number of successes we would expect if we repeated this sampling process many times.
\[
E(X) = n \cdot \frac{k}{N}
\]

n * (k / N)


population_size <- 15
successes_pop   <- 4
sample_size     <- 2

  (successes_pop / population_size)

expected_value



Variance
\[
\operatorname{Var}(X)=n \cdot \frac{k}{N}\left(1 - \frac{k}{N}\right)\frac{N - n}{N - 1}
\]

sample_size *
  (successes_pop / population_size) *
  (1 - successes_pop / population_size) *
  ((population_size - sample_size) /
     (population_size - 1))
